questions.stem: Minh, 63, is in a GP clinic with jaundice, spider naevi and palmar erythema. You suspect portal hypertension and want to examine for an enlarged spleen while he lies supine with his abdomen exposed. How should you palpate for the spleen?
options: Start in the right iliac fossa, advance towards the left costal margin on inspiration
Start at the left costal margin and move down towards the left iliac fossa
Start in the left iliac fossa and move straight up towards the left costal margin
Start in the epigastrium and move laterally along the left costal margin
questions.why: The spleen enlarges down and medially towards the right iliac fossa. Starting there and working diagonally towards the left costal margin, with the patient breathing in to bring the tip down, means you will not miss a large spleen.
notes: Starting under the costal margin can put your hand over a massive spleen, so you miss its edge completely.
The spleen grows diagonally towards the right iliac fossa, not straight down, so a vertical line from the left iliac fossa can miss it.
The epigastrium is not where an enlarging spleen extends, and moving along the costal margin does not follow its path of enlargement.

questions.stem: Minh's HCV RNA is 1.8 x 10^6 IU/mL. He is jaundiced (bilirubin 60 µmol/L), with albumin 29 g/L, INR 1.4 and platelets 120 x 10^9/L. He has no ascites or encephalopathy, which gives Child-Pugh class B. He wants to start treatment as soon as possible. What is the most appropriate next step in treating his hepatitis C?
options: GP prescribes sofosbuvir/velpatasvir for 12 weeks, and checks HCV RNA 12 weeks after
GP prescribes glecaprevir/pibrentasvir for 8 weeks, and checks HCV RNA 12 weeks after
Urgent hepatology referral for specialist-led antiviral therapy, usually with ribavirin
Hold off antiviral therapy until a FibroScan has confirmed and staged the cirrhosis
questions.why: GPs can prescribe direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) on the PBS, but decompensated cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B or C) needs a specialist to lead treatment. The usual regimen is sofosbuvir/velpatasvir plus ribavirin for 12 weeks, alongside variceal screening and transplant assessment.
notes: Sofosbuvir/velpatasvir is the right drug, but a GP should not treat decompensated cirrhosis alone. He needs ribavirin, close monitoring and hepatology care.
Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir contains a protease inhibitor, which is contraindicated in decompensated (Child-Pugh B or C) cirrhosis because of the risk of liver injury.
Jaundice, low albumin and a raised INR already show decompensation. Waiting for elastography would delay urgent specialist care and does not change the need to refer.

questions.stem: Minh, 63, has untreated chronic hepatitis C. Over the past year he has had about five episodes of a bumpy, non-itchy, painless rash on his lower legs, each settling within a week. It is palpable purpura. Platelets are 120 x 10^9/L and INR is 1.4. Which mechanism best explains the rash?
options: Bleeding into the skin from thrombocytopenia caused by splenic sequestration
Deficiency of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors from impaired liver synthesis
IgA immune complex deposition in dermal small vessels, as in IgA vasculitis
Rheumatoid factor–IgG–HCV immune complexes deposit in small vessels and fix complement
questions.why: In mixed cryoglobulinaemia, HCV drives B cells to make IgM rheumatoid factor. This binds IgG and HCV antigen to form complexes that precipitate in the cooler, dependent leg vessels and activate complement (low C4), causing a palpable leukocytoclastic vasculitis.
notes: Spontaneous skin bleeding usually needs platelets well below 50, and purpura from thrombocytopenia is flat, not palpable.
Coagulopathy causes bruising and ecchymoses, not recurrent palpable purpura, and an INR of 1.4 is only mildly raised.
IgA vasculitis is mainly a disease of children after infection. The small-vessel vasculitis linked to hepatitis C is mixed cryoglobulinaemia.

questions.stem: Minh, 63, has decompensated hepatitis C cirrhosis with a palpable spleen and platelets of 120. The hepatologist plans a gastroscopy to screen for oesophageal varices. At the lower oesophagus, varices form at an anastomosis between which veins?
options: Superior rectal vein and middle and inferior rectal veins
Paraumbilical veins and superficial epigastric veins
Left gastric vein and oesophageal tributaries of the azygos vein
Splenic vein and left renal vein
questions.why: In portal hypertension, blood is diverted from the left gastric vein (portal system) into the oesophageal veins that drain to the azygos vein (systemic system). The submucosal veins of the lower oesophagus dilate into varices, which can bleed severely.
notes: This is the portosystemic anastomosis in the anorectal region, which forms rectal varices, not oesophageal ones.
This anastomosis at the umbilicus produces caput medusae, not oesophageal varices.
A splenorenal shunt can form on its own in portal hypertension, but it is not the anastomosis that forms oesophageal varices.
